headline: How Hidden Genes Helped Invaders Thrive
meta_description: Scientists discover brown tree snakes carry far more genetic diversity than expected, explaining their devastating invasion of Guam.
summary_short: Researchers find 19,000 hidden genetic variations in brown tree snakes, concentrated in immunity and smell genes, explaining their explosive spread across Guam.
body:
A small handful of brown tree snakes that likely arrived in Guam after World War II, possibly stowed aboard military cargo planes, somehow defied biological expectation and multiplied into one of the world's most notorious invasions. New research reveals the answer: these reptiles carried far more genetic diversity than scientists had realized. Using advanced long-read DNA sequencing, University at Buffalo researchers identified more than 19,000 structural variants in the snakes' genome—large genetic differences involving duplicated, deleted, or rearranged DNA segments. Remarkably, these variations clustered in genes controlling immunity and smell, potentially giving the population unexpected advantages for survival, adaptation, and rapid growth despite their inbred origins.

The discovery challenges assumptions about what limited founding populations can achieve. Normally, when only a few individuals establish a population in a new environment, severe genetic bottlenecks should cripple their ability to adapt. Yet Guam's brown tree snakes thrived so completely that some areas now host densities as high as 30,000 snakes per square mile, driving native forest birds toward extinction and causing hundreds of annual power outages by climbing utility poles. The snakes' heightened olfactory diversity may also explain a behavioral shift: while brown tree snakes commonly eat each other in their native Australian and Pacific ranges, they rarely do so in Guam.

Beyond its troubling implications for invasive species control, the research offers unexpected hope. Scientists now suspect that endangered species with small or highly inbred populations may possess more genetic flexibility than previously believed. As researchers noted, older DNA sequencing tools could only detect tiny individual base-pair changes, missing the larger structural variants that actually shape most genetic variation. This discovery demonstrates how advancing technology reveals hidden complexity in life itself.
quick_facts: Brown tree snakes likely arrived in Guam after World War II aboard military cargo
Researchers found 19,000+ structural variants in snake genomes, mostly in immune and smell genes
Some Guam areas now host 30,000 snakes per square mile
Study published July 24, 2026 in Science Advances by University at Buffalo
